name: Nennius
knownFor: Named in its own prologue and apology as the writer of the Historia Brittonum, a Latin history of the Britons. It tells of Vortigern, the bishop Germanus of Auxerre, Saint Patrick and Arthur's twelve battles. Its author is disputed.
dates: The book's own dates differ. The prologue in J. A. Giles's translation gives 858, the twenty-fourth year of Mervin, king of the Britons. Its list of years reaches 976, the fifth year of Edmund, king of the Angles. Another passage counts the year of writing as 547 years after the Saxons came in 447. John Williams ab Ithel dates a first edition to 674. Louis Duchesne places the pseudo-Nennius in the ninth century. No source used here gives the writer's birth or death.
place: Among the Britons; W. H. Stevenson calls Nennius a Welsh writer
role: Compiler and historian of the Britons; by his own account a disciple of Elbotus

keyWorks.title: Historia Brittonum (History of the Britons)
keyWorks.about: a Latin history of the Britons. Its writer says he drew on Roman annals, the chronicles of the sacred fathers, the annals of the Scots and Saxons and his people's traditions. It runs from the ages of the world and Brutus through Roman Britain, Vortigern and the coming of the Saxons. Then come the bishop Germanus, Saint Patrick, Arthur's battles and the genealogies of the English kings. A heading in J. A. Giles's text says it was edited by Mark the anchorite

traces: John Williams ab Ithel says the copy of the Annales Cambriae he calls A, Harleian 3859, is set without a title inside a Nennius manuscript.
Hugh Williams says the Annales Cambriae's entry for the battle of Badon looks like a mistaken borrowing from this book.
W. H. Stevenson says the British name of Thanet in Asser's Life of King Alfred may come from it. In his notes he calls it derived, no doubt, from this book.
Whitley Stokes prints extracts from it, from Harleian 3859, among the early documents on Saint Patrick.
Hugh Williams says Geoffrey of Monmouth quotes from it, naming Gildas as its author.
remembered: Louis Duchesne and James Raine call its writer the pseudo-Nennius.
John Williams ab Ithel writes of the author of the book of Nennius as living at a later period. He notes that this author made Badon the twelfth of Arthur's battles.

W. H. Stevenson tells of a passage added to Asser's Life in William Camden's edition. It claimed that Oxford's university existed before Alfred and kept usages sanctioned by Germanus, Gildas, Nennius and Kentigern. Stevenson calls it an interpolation, made to prove Oxford older than Cambridge.
Stevenson notes that Archbishop Ussher used eleven manuscripts of Nennius.

uncertain: Its author is disputed. The prologue and the apology name Nennius, disciple of Elbotus, and Hugh Williams and W. H. Stevenson write of the book as his. A heading in J. A. Giles's text says it was edited by Mark the anchorite, a holy bishop of the Britons. Louis Duchesne lists a Vatican copy under Mark's name and calls the writer pseudo-Nennius, as James Raine does. Hugh Williams notes that some copies give the book to Gildas.

The book's own dates differ, and so do its copies. Giles notes that hardly two manuscripts give the list of years alike. John Williams ab Ithel reads a line of the Vatican copy as dating a first edition to 674. He thinks a younger man probably compiled the genealogies, which reach as late as 738.

Elbotus. Giles's note makes him Elvod, bishop of Bangor in 755, who first adopted the new Easter cycle in the Welsh church. The Annales Cambriae put the change of Easter among the Britons in the year their editor reckons as 768, made by Elbodug. They put the death of Elbodg, archbishop of Gwynedd, in 809. One of their manuscripts calls him bishop of Gwynedd.

Arthur. Giles's text gives nine hundred and forty killed by Arthur's hand at Badon. John Williams ab Ithel gives 960, and another version 840. Some manuscripts, Giles notes, add that Arthur went to Jerusalem and made a cross there.

The order of its parts. Giles notes that some manuscripts place the passage on the growing Saxons and Arthur after the account of Patrick. He takes the tale of Brutus as older than Geoffrey, unless, he adds, it was put into the original work later.
